solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Marriage followed by a hefty do, off a TV show

indicators.note: something that has gone off is spoilt or out of its proper state, so these letters must be rearranged
one thing followed by another puts the second piece straight after the first

blocks.note: a match is a marriage or pairing
the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wedding with a big party afterwards, then someone disappears from a television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: MATCH OF THE DAY is the BBC's long-running football highlights programme; the comma splits the clue so 'off' works on the phrase before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the title of a famous British television football highlights programme, so it is literally a programme broadcast on television.

clue.text: Test by Henry securing university entrance

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece wraps round another
standing by something means being next to it, so the pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British cars
U is the standard abbreviation for university
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: An exam taken by someone called Henry that wins him a place at university.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOT is Britain's yearly vehicle safety test. 'Entrance' is not about getting into university here; it is an opening, MO(U)T + H.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouth is an opening or way in, as with the mouth of a cave or river, so it is an entrance.

clue.text: Accessories of netting on top of silk

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter
in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

blocks.note: netting an animal is trapping it
the first letter of silk

explanation.surface: Fashion accessories made from mesh laid over silk fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Netting' reads as a material, but it is the verb: catching in a net.
explanation.definitionFit: Trappings are the outward decorations and adornments that go with something, much like accessories added to an outfit.

clue.text: Plant, entirely lead-free

indicators.note: free of its lead means without its opening letter

blocks.note: wholly means entirely

explanation.surface: A plant that contains no lead at all, as in the metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead-free' suggests petrol or paint, but lead here is the first letter: WHOLLY without W.
explanation.definitionFit: Holly is an evergreen shrub with prickly leaves and red berries, a common example of a plant.

clue.text: This heats up Spooner’s curious lover

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

blocks.note: curious means prying; it takes the opening sound of the next word
a lover of something is a fan; it takes the opening sound of the previous word

explanation.surface: Something that excites a strangely nosy admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heats up' sounds like arousing someone, but the definition is a kitchen utensil: prying fan with P and F swapped.
explanation.definitionFit: A frying pan is a shallow cooking vessel placed on a hob to warm and cook food, so it is a thing that heats up.

clue.text: Covers up from middle of the day in Rome

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter

blocks.note: the central letter of the
the Ides was a fixed day in the Roman calendar, around the middle of the month

explanation.surface: Something hides away from the midday heat in Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle of the day' looks like noon, but it takes the middle letter of 'the' only; the Ides of March is the famous one.
explanation.definitionFit: To hide something is to conceal it from view, which is what covering it up achieves.

clue.text: One bringing meat to feed animals

indicators.note: food that feeds an animal goes inside it, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: deer are animals
liver is offal eaten as meat

explanation.surface: A zookeeper bringing in meat for the animals' feed.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a keeper, but the keeper is only the definition; the animals are DEER, which would hardly want LIVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A deliverer is a person who conveys goods to someone, so it is one who brings things.

clue.text: Sing melody, ripping off male cuckoo

indicators.note: ripping something off tears it away, so a letter is removed
cuckoo means crazy, so the remaining letters go into a mad new order

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for male, the letter to be removed

explanation.surface: A cuckoo sings its tune, and a male bird steals someone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cuckoo' tempts as the bird, but it is the anagram signal. Remove M from MELODY and rearrange ELODY.
explanation.definitionFit: To yodel is to sing in a style that switches rapidly between chest voice and falsetto, associated with the Alps.

clue.text: Extremely cut off, a city goes under

indicators.note: in a down clue, what goes under another piece is written below it

blocks.note: to sever is to cut off
Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A city totally isolated sinks beneath the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes under' suggests a flooded or bankrupt city, but in a down clue it places the city below the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Severely is used to mean to a great or harsh degree, as in severely damaged, which matches extremely.

clue.text: Pure ecstasy filling boy next to girl

indicators.note: a filling goes inside something, so one piece sits within another
being next to something means the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: Una is a girl's name
Lloyd is a boy's name
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Sheer bliss fills a boy sitting beside a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The order is reversed from the clue: the girl comes first, then the boy with E inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Unalloyed literally describes metal not mixed with another, and figuratively means complete or unmixed, as pure does.

clue.text: House deposit

blocks.note: first meaning: a small house, such as a gatekeeper's or hunting cabin
second meaning: to place or leave something somewhere for safekeeping

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it sounds like a down payment on a home; the two words are separate meanings, one a noun and one a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for a small dwelling and a verb meaning to put something in a place, as in lodging money with a bank.

clue.text: Content of pop emptied through straw

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving only the outer letters
something going through another runs inside it

blocks.note: hay is dried grass, much like straw
the outer letters of pop

explanation.surface: A fizzy drink being sucked up through a straw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as the noun (what is inside the bottle) but is the adjective meaning satisfied.
explanation.definitionFit: Being content means feeling satisfied and at ease, a mild form of being glad or pleased.

clue.text: Architect, beastly about large country home?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: John Nash designed Regent Street and Brighton Pavilion
beastly means nasty or vile
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: An architect being horrid about a big house in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country home' looks like a manor house; the question mark warns that country means country music.
explanation.definitionFit: Nashville in Tennessee is the centre of the country music industry, often called its home or capital.

clue.text: Periodical printed in Bavaria and used in state exam

indicators.note: something used in another is put inside it

blocks.note: to state is to say
und is German for and, and Bavaria is in Germany
an exam paper

explanation.surface: A magazine produced in Bavaria that a state examination makes use of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bavaria' signals a German word, and the German for 'and' is UND; the self-reference to this very Sunday Times puzzle is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sunday paper is a newspaper issued every week on one day, so it is a regularly published printed periodical.

clue.text: Food’s roasting still

blocks.note: snap is a northern English word for a packed lunch, plus the 's
roasting means very hot

explanation.surface: The food is still in the oven roasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as an adverb, but it is the noun, a still photograph. Snap is a dialect word, especially in Yorkshire, for a worker's packed food.
explanation.definitionFit: A still is a single photograph, and a snapshot is a quickly taken informal photograph.

clue.text: White stone flower made in an experiment?

blocks.note: an experiment is done in a lab, read as 'a lab'
the aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A white flower bred artificially by scientists.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsy: a flower made in an experiment is 'a lab aster'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster is a fine-grained translucent mineral, usually white, carved into ornaments and statues.

clue.text: TV broadcast with top aria singer

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A television transmission of a leading singer performing a fine aria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the TV scene so well that it hides its job of mixing the letters of TV and TOP ARIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Luciano Pavarotti was a celebrated Italian operatic tenor, one of the most famous vocalists of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Sign an auditor’s letter

indicators.note: an auditor is literally a listener, so what follows is as heard rather than written

blocks.note: the letter Q is pronounced the same way

explanation.surface: Signing a letter sent by an accountant who checks the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' looks like a financial inspector; read as a hearer it turns the letter Q into a word that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is a signal prompting someone to act or speak, as in an actor's cue, so it is a sign.

clue.text: Wild vicar full of hot air spoilt wedding serenade

indicators.note: being full of something means holding it inside
wild means out of control, so the letters break out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
taken as written

explanation.surface: A furious, pompous vicar ruined the music at a wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: A charivari is an old folk custom of banging pans outside newlyweds' house, a deliberately discordant mock serenade.
explanation.definitionFit: A charivari was a noisy, discordant mock serenade of pots and kettles performed for a newly married couple.

clue.text: A piece of thread Sherlock notices

indicators.note: a piece of something is a portion of it, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes spots a scrap of thread at a crime scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' looks like Sherlock's verb, but it is the noun: printed announcements.
explanation.definitionFit: Ads, short for advertisements, are public announcements in print, which notices also are.

clue.text: Celebration, nervy, as Iran is involved

indicators.note: involved means tangled or convoluted, so the letters are twisted into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A festive occasion turns tense because Iran has become involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is involved' reads as Iran joining in, but it tangles the letters of NERVY and AS IRAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An anniversary is the yearly return of a notable date, typically marked with a party or celebration.

clue.text: Browning fan’s newspaper article accepted by poet, unfinished

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter goes
what is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a bard is a poet; it loses its last letter
the definite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece by an admirer of the poet Robert Browning, published by another poet but never completed.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning the Victorian poet is the obvious reading, and the other poet in the clue backs it up, but browning here means getting a tan.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunbather lies out to tan the skin, so is a devotee of getting brown in the sun.

clue.text: Church books go on about Old Nick

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another
in a down clue, pieces that go on another sit above it

blocks.note: NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible
O is the abbreviation for old
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: The church's records keep going on about the Devil, Old Nick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Nick' is a nickname for the Devil, but the two words are split: Old is O and nick is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nick is a small cut or indentation in an edge or surface, and a notch is exactly that kind of mark.

clue.text: The way to perform a greeting

blocks.note: how means the way something is done
to do is to perform

explanation.surface: Instructions on the correct manner of saying hello.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How do' is a northern English greeting, short for how do you do.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a casual salutation used in northern England when meeting someone, a shortened how do you do.

clue.text: Stage play’s latest bloomer

indicators.note: the latest part of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: a dais is a raised platform or stage
the final letter of play

explanation.surface: An actor makes a blunder in the newest stage play.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer in British English is a blunder, which the theatre surface exploits; here it is something that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A daisy is a common flowering plant, and anything that produces flowers can playfully be called a bloomer.

clue.text: Bar being raised by South Africa’s backs

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word lifts its letters to read bottom to top

blocks.note: a rod is a bar
SA is the abbreviation for South Africa

explanation.surface: A rugby talking point: the standard being lifted by the Springbok full-backs.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby the backs are positions, but here backs is the definition, the plural of the Latin dorsum.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorsa is the plural of dorsum, the anatomical term for the rear surface of a body or organ.

clue.text: Territory that borders a country

indicators.note: to border something is to lie along its edges, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: yon is an old word for that, as in yon hill
the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: A region lying along the frontier of a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yukon does border a country, Alaska's USA, which makes the surface feel literal; but the country is the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: The Yukon is one of Canada's three northern territories, a federal division rather than a province.

clue.text: Tenor and the rest start in Opera backing group

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
backing up means going backwards, so the letters run in reverse order

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for tenor
etc, et cetera, means and the rest
the first letter of Opera

explanation.surface: A tenor and his fellow musicians starting out in an opera's backing group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing group' reads as a band behind a singer, but backing is the reversal and the definition is just group.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is a set of eight musicians or singers performing together, so it is a musical group.

clue.text: Design on paper with name placed in a box

indicators.note: placing something in another puts it inside

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written
a term is a name for something
an ark is a chest or box, as in the Ark of the Covenant

explanation.surface: A drawing on paper with someone's name written inside a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A box' must stay together as one container: the name goes between the article and the box, not inside the box alone. An ark can be any chest, as in the Ark of the Covenant.
explanation.definitionFit: A watermark is a faint image impressed into paper during manufacture, visible when held up to light.

clue.text: Hurt by love, one’s protected by people coming together

indicators.note: something protected is shielded on all sides, so it sits inside another piece

blocks.note: to hurt is to harm
love is zero in tennis, written O
a people is a nation
one is I and the 's is is

explanation.surface: Someone wounded by love finds shelter in a community that unites.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s in "one's" is read as the verb 'is', so one's supplies two letters that sit just after the first letter of the people.
explanation.definitionFit: Harmonisation is the act of bringing different things into agreement or alignment, which is a coming together.
